title: Besiege Wei to Rescue Zhao
text:
In 354 BC the state of Wei sent its army against Zhao and besieged the Zhao capital, Handan. Zhao begged Qi for help. King Wei of Qi wanted to make Sun Bin commander, but Sun Bin declined because he had been mutilated and branded as a criminal, so Tian Ji led the army and Sun Bin rode along in a covered cart as adviser.

Tian Ji meant to march straight to Handan and fight the Wei army there. Sima Qian records Sun Bin's objection: to untangle a snarled thread you do not pull at it with your fists, and to break up a fight you do not join the blows. Wei's best troops, he argued, were all at Handan, leaving only the old and weak at home. Qi should march on the Wei capital, Daliang, and seize its roads. Wei would have to abandon the siege to save itself.

Tian Ji agreed. When the Wei army heard that its capital was threatened, it left Handan and hurried home. Exhausted after the long march, it met the Qi army at Guiling and was heavily defeated. The phrase "besiege Wei to rescue Zhao" became one of the classic Chinese strategic sayings.
lesson: Instead of meeting a problem where it is strongest, look for the place the other side must protect. Pressure there can resolve the original fight without fighting it.
people: Sun Bin, Tian Ji, Pang Juan
location: Handan and Guiling (modern Hebei and Henan, China)
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 65
